info.bio: Ramones fue una influyente banda de Punk rock formada en Forest Hills, en el barrio de Queens, Nueva York, Estados Unidos en 1974. Fueron los pioneros del naciente punk rock, un sonido simple, minimalista y repetitivo que evitaba la musicalidad de los solos de guitarra de las bandas de los 70. Consistía básicamente en un sonido crudo, rápido y directo con influencias directas en los grupos rockabilly de los 50, pero fundamentalmente de bandas como New York Dolls, MC5 y The Stooges.

scenes.name: Punk rock (1976-77)
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».

scenes.name: Punk neoyorquino del CBGB
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».

scenes.name: New wave neoyorquina
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: 1976 es un año bisagra: los sellos independientes revitalizan la industria y nuevos géneros la escena, una revolución comparable a la de 1966. Los jóvenes de los setenta, sin sueños tras la derrota de la contracultura, canalizan su aburrimiento en un sonido crudo emparentado con el garage. Nueva York es la capital: el CBGB's y el Max's Kansas City. Patti Smith, Richard Hell (el profeta: «Blank Generation» y la ética punk), Television (Marquee Moon, que define la estética de la new wave), Tom Verlaine, y los Ramones, que tocan rock'n'roll inepto a velocidad supersónica e inventan el género más importante del último cuarto de siglo.

podcast.body: D.D. Ramone and John Cummings decided to form a band in 1974 after getting drunk after work one day. Neither of them knew anything about music at the time, but they were driven by a desire to create it. "That was 1974, and neither guy knew the first thing about music, but they didn't care."

podcast.title: Band Formation (1974)
podcast.body: The four original members connected through a series of introductions: Jeffrey Hyman (Joey) met Douglas Colvin (Dee Dee) at a Sniper show; Douglas introduced Jeffrey to John Cummings (Johnny); and Johnny introduced them to Tommy Erdelyi (Tommy), who already knew Joey from the neighborhood. Tommy suggested they form a band, offering to manage them, which they did. "It was Tommy that told the other three guys that they should form a band, all advise and manage. And so they did."

podcast.title: CBGB Debut (August 16, 1974)
podcast.body: On August 16, 1974, The Ramones played their first gig at CBGB, opening for Television or possibly two other bands. The audience was minimal, with only six people (plus Hilly and his dog) present. They played 20 songs in 17 minutes, characterized by a primitive, ragged, and goofy appearance. "On August 16th, 1974, the Ramones opened for television, or they might have been opening for two other bands. No one really remembers because there were just six people in the bar."

podcast.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
podcast.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."

podcast.title: First CBGB Show (August 1974)
podcast.body: When the Ramones played their inaugural show at CBGB in August 1974, their performance was described as "absolutely terrible." Their distinctive haircuts, leather jackets, and shared last names, combined with their ability to play 15 songs in 20 minutes, led many to question if they were serious or if it was a joke. "When they played their first show at CBGB in August 1974, they were absolutely terrible."

podcast.title: Early Label Rejection & Sire Signing (1975)
podcast.body: The Ramones were signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records in 1975 after he discovered them in a Manhattan bar. Other labels refused to sign them because they were considered "too weird," played "too fast," were "too amateurish," and "too funny looking." Mainstream rock radio also rejected them, seeing them as a joke. "back then, nobody wanted to touch the Ramones. They were just too weird. They played too fast. They were too amateurish. podcast.title: Backstage Window Encounter (July 4, 1976)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash recounted how he, Johnny Rotten, and members of the Sex Pistols met The Ramones backstage at the Roundhouse by throwing a rock at a window. Johnny Ramone stuck his head out, and the British punks introduced themselves, being subsequently pulled up through the window in a "human chain" to get in. srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Conquest of England (July 4 & 6, 1976)
podcast.body: The Ramones played two pivotal shows in London, first at the Roundhouse (capacity 2,000) on America's bicentennial, and then at Dingwalls two nights later. Despite their European record company trying to cancel gigs, the band delivered explosive performances. These concerts were England's "first proper exposure" to US-style punk rock and are credited with transforming nearly every major player in the burgeoning British punk rock scene, including members of the Sex Pistols, The Clash, The Pretenders, The Damned, and Generation X. "And over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th, 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

podcast.title: First Album Release (Mid-1976)
podcast.body: The Ramones released their first album approximately six months after Patti Smith's debut "Horses" in November 1975. They were a key band in the early New York City punk scene. "and a good six months before the Ramones released their first album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First British Show (1976) - Catalyst for UK Punk
podcast.body: The Ramones played their first British show at the Roundhouse in London on July 4, 1976, the date of the American Bicentennial. This concert, which was attended by members of the Sex Pistols and The Clash, was a major catalyst in the development of British punk rock, with the band being treated "like Royal Teal" and inspiring a new generation of musicians. "And from that night on, the UK music scene was really never the same. The Ramones became a major catalyst in the development of British punk rock."

podcast.title: Influence in England (1976)
podcast.body: Despite their dislike for Europe, The Ramones were well-received there, particularly in England. Their performance at the CBGV Rock Festival Showcase Auditions in 1975 introduced them to the British press, and their 1976 tour in England greatly influenced punk bands like Generation X, whose member Billy Idol considered them "brilliant." "When the Ramones went to England in 1976, a punk band called Generation X Which was started by someone called Billy Idol saw them play Billy Idol said he thought they were brilliant and it influenced how his band chose to play."

The band felt like "royalty" upon arrival, noting the shift from selling out CBGB's to playing for 3,000 kids already "tuned in." "No one could have known it at the time, but this was one of the most influential gigs in the history of rock."

podcast.title: Attempted Crossover with "Rock 'n' Roll High School" (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, The Ramones appeared in the B-movie *Rock 'n' Roll High School*, produced by Roger Corman. The film capitalized on the late 70s musical movie craze and starred P.J. Soles as Riff Randall. The Ramones, though not the first choice (Cheap Trick and Todd Rundgren were considered), provided a "very punchy theme song" and looked the part of youth rebels. The movie was a critical success and modest box office earner, intended as a mainstream crossover vehicle for the band into the 1980s. "A claimed by critics and a modest box office success upon its release in 1979, Rock and Roll High School should have been the ticket for the Ramones too at last make a mainstream crossover into the 1980s."

podcast.title: Volatile Recording Sessions with Phil Spector (1980)
podcast.body: For their *End of the Century* album, The Ramones worked with legendary producer Phil Spector, known for his "Wall of Sound" but also his perfectionism and violent temper. Spector had pursued the band for years, seeing their "punk melodicism" as a replica of his classic sound. The band agreed to work with him to expand their fanbase but regretted the decision due to Spector locking them in the studio, demanding endless takes, and allegedly holding Joey and Dee Dee Ramone hostage at gunpoint. "A decision the Ramones came to regret when Specter locked them in the studio and made them do take after take."

podcast.title: Fractured Skull Attack (August 1983) – Street Brawl Led to Brain Surgery, Later Distrust of Doctors, and Death
podcast.body: In August 1983, Johnny Ramone became involved in a brawl with Seth Maclin of a band called Sub Zero Construction on the street outside Johnny's East Village apartment at 4am. Johnny was beaten to the pavement and kicked in the head. He was rushed to hospital with a fractured skull and required brain surgery. He recovered, but the incident left him deeply distrustful of doctors. When he later began experiencing abdominal pain — roughly 15 years after the attack — his mistrust caused him to delay seeking treatment. The abdominal pain was aggressive prostate cancer that spread throughout his body. Chemotherapy failed, and Johnny died on September 15, 2004. "Had he not been beaten up in the summer of 1983 and still trusted doctors?"

podcast.body: In 1987, founding Ramones bassist Dee Dee Ramone abruptly left the band to pursue a solo hip-hop career under the name Dee Dee King, recording a track called "Funky Man." The attempt was widely considered disastrous. He tried to re-enter punk rock but never achieved significant success in any subsequent project. He died of a heroin overdose on June 5, 2002. "Dee Dee Ramon, the guy who played bass in all those legendary early Ramones songs, trying to be a rapper. Terrible career move, dude."

podcast.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
podcast.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."

podcast.body: After their appearance at Lollapalooza in the summer of 1996, The Ramones played their last show in Hollywood, concluding a career that spanned 2,263 performances and finally receiving deserved recognition for their contributions before the deaths of Joey and Johnny Ramone. "After that summer, they would play their last show in Hollywood, bringing the curtain down on a career that included 2,263 shows."

podcast.title: Mainstream Comeback and Lollapalooza 1996
podcast.body: The outpouring of affection and attention from a new generation brought The Ramones back into the mainstream, culminating in their appearance as main stage stars at the Lollapalooza festival in 1996. "The outpouring of affection and attention was so strong that by 1996, they were one of the mainstaged stars of the Lollapalooza festival."

podcast.title: Cancer Recurrence Post-Surgery (December 2000 - April 2001)
podcast.body: The severe hip fracture Joey Ramone sustained necessitated surgery, which required him to be taken off his anti-lymphoma medication. This interruption caused his lymphoma to come out of remission, ultimately preventing him from ever returning home from the hospital. "And for that, he needed to be taken off his anti-limfoma meds. The lymphoma came out of remission, and Joey wasn't ever able to go home again."

podcast.title: OCD-Induced Fall and Hip Fracture (December 2000)
podcast.body: On December 30, 2000, Joey Ramone, who had struggled with obsessive-compulsive disorder since childhood, was overcome by an intense urge to check if he had properly closed a door across town. Despite fighting the compulsion, his OCD demanded action, leading him to venture out on a cold, icy New York City day. During his journey, he slipped and fell, fracturing his hip due to bones weakened and brittle from chemotherapy treatments for lymphoma. "On December 30, 2000, he was overcome with a feeling that he hadn't closed the door properly on the other side of town." "On his way to that door, wherever it was, Joey slipped and fell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Deaths of Original Members (2001-2014)
podcast.body: The original lineup of the Ramones tragically passed away over a 13-year period: Joey Ramone in 2001, Dee Dee Ramone in 2002, Johnny Ramone in 2004, and Tommy Ramone in 2014, marking the end of an era for the seminal punk band. "He was the first of the original Ramones to die. Base player DD Ramon died of a heroin overdose the following summer. Whereas Johnny Ramon lost his fight with prostate cancer in September 2004, and drummer Tommy Ramon was taken by Bile Duck Cancer in the summer of 2014."

podcast.title: Final Moments and Last Song (April 2001)
podcast.body: On April 15, 2001, a month before his 50th birthday, Joey Ramone, nearing the end of his life at New York's Presbyterian Hospital, asked to listen to U2's song "In a Little While" from their album "All That You Can't Leave Behind" on a boombox beside his bed. Those present reported that he passed away just as the song concluded. "He asked to listen to a song in the boom box that was next to his bed at New York's Presbyterian Hospital. It was you two's in a little while, a song from the all that you can't leave behind album. Those who were with him at the time say that just as the song ended, Joey passed away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's OCD – Lifelong Battle Barely Acknowledged, Finally Confirmed on 2002 Solo Album
podcast.body: Joey Ramone suffered from obsessive-compulsive disorder that preceded the formation of the Ramones and is cited by those close to him as a major reason he was so shy, awkward, and withdrawn in private. His OCD manifested in compulsive repetitive behaviors — stepping off and on a curb dozens of times, repeating words over and over driven by voices in his head — and he was hospitalized at least once when it became unmanageable. Despite this, Joey vehemently denied having OCD whenever it was raised publicly, and the subject was almost never discussed. As he came to terms with his cancer and mortality, he relented slightly, and in the song "Like a Drug I Never Did Before" on his 2002 posthumous solo album *Don't Worry About Me*, he addressed his lifelong battle with OCD — the only time he ever mentioned it in his music. "This is the only time he ever brought it up in his music."

podcast.body: Douglas Colvin (Dee Dee Ramone) grew up as an "army brat" in a profoundly unhappy military family, where domestic violence was common. podcast.title: Dee Dee Ramone's Mental Health and Mood Swings
podcast.body: Dee Dee Ramone was reportedly diagnosed as bipolar but chose not to seek treatment. He was known as a "very scary dude prone to huge mood swings." "There's one story that he was diagnosed as being bipolar, but he didn't seek any treatment for it."

podcast.title: Defining Image and Sound of Punk
podcast.body: The Ramones significantly contributed to the popularization of punk rock, becoming "the ultimate punks on so many different levels." They were distinctive for their uniform of leather jackets, t-shirts, and torn jeans, and for playing songs that distilled 60s bubblegum pop to its essence, delivered with immense volume and speed. "The Ramones helped of course. In their uniform of leather jackets and t-shirts and torn jeans and playing songs that were basically 60s bubblegum at the volume and speed of a jet engine, well they became the ultimate punks on so many different levels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defining Punk's Form and Sound
podcast.body: The Ramones were instrumental in solidifying the identity of punk rock. They eschewed poetry, long solos, and experimentation in favor of playing fast, loud, and without overthinking. Their songs, typically two minutes long with three chords and absurd lyrics about girls, baseball, drugs, or adolescent violence, aimed for immediate impact rather than deep meaning, effectively giving punk its definitive form, sound, and speed. "No buscaban significado, sólo impacto, y con ellos el punk ya tenía forma sonido y velocidad."

podcast.title: Disdain for CBGB
podcast.body: The Ramones themselves didn't think highly of CBGB initially, finding the stage too small, Hilly Crystal unhygienic, and the club plagued by rats and mice. They also found the clientele unpleasant, noting patrons would relieve themselves in corners due to the awful bathrooms. "Now to be fair, the Ramones didn't think too much of CBGB either. podcast.title: Dislike of Avant-Garde and Europe
podcast.body: The Ramones actively disliked the avant-garde scene and demonstrated a strong aversion to European culture during a tour with the Talking Heads, disliking the food, only wanting to hear English, and refusing to leave their tour bus even to see Stonehenge. Danny Fields, their manager, famously compared taking them to Europe to "taking Archie Bunker to the Vatican," emphasizing their populist, not artistic, nature. "They were not part of the avant-garde scene at all, they did not like it."

podcast.title: Early Rehearsals and Lineup Changes
podcast.body: The Ramones' first rehearsal took place at Johnny's apartment with bassist Richie Stern, who quickly quit. A more formal rehearsal followed on January 24th, 1974, at the Performance Studio, with Jeffrey on drums, Johnny on guitar, and Douglas on lead vocals and bass. They were initially "terrible," unable to play their instruments well or covers, only knowing their own simple songs. Douglas quickly lost his voice, and Jeffrey, a loud but slow drummer, moved to vocals, leading to Tommy eventually taking over drums in July 1974. "They were not ready, not even close. podcast.title: Early Songwriting Themes
podcast.body: The Ramones began writing songs about what they knew, which largely involved being "near-to-wells" and "hoodlums" who were better at "hanging out, drinking, getting in fist fights, and doing drugs" than actual crime. Their early songs often began with the phrase "I don't want to," such as "I Don't Want To Get Involved With You," "I Don't Want To Walk Around With You," "I Don't Want To Be Learned, I Don't Want To Be Tamed," and "I Don't Want To Go Down To The Basement." "They started to write about what they knew, which was, well what exactly? Well, they were all a bunch of near-to-wells, a bunch of hoodlums."

podcast.title: Formation and Lineup Change – Drummer to Frontman
podcast.body: The Ramones were formed in early 1974, with Jeff Hyman (later Joey Ramone) on drums, John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) on guitar, and Douglas Colvin (later D.D. Ramone) on bass. Due to Jeff's powerful, fast drumming style and his superior singing ability, he transitioned to lead vocalist, with a friend named Tommy taking over on drums using a basic $100 kit. It was alleged that he would get drunk and frequent these institutions, stating that "the girls were all loose there," and supposedly fell in love with a woman who received weekly electro-shock therapy. This attraction is linked to his own experiences with mental health, which also influenced lyrics he wrote for the Ramones, such as "Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment." "Apparently Joey had a thing for a while for girls from mental hospitals."

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's Capitalism
podcast.body: Despite embodying the image of an "archetypical punk," Joey Ramone was, in fact, a hardcore capitalist. In the years leading up to his death, he became very skilled at stock trading over the internet. He reportedly amassed a considerable fortune by diligently following the Wall Street Journal, watching CNBC, and utilizing his online trading account.

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's Death and Memorial
podcast.body: Diagnosed with lymphoma in 1995, Joey Ramone's cancer worsened after he broke his hip in a fall in late 2000, which necessitated coming off his chemotherapy. He died on April 15, 2001, just one month before his 50th birthday. The corner of East Second Street and Bowery, near CBGB and his last apartment, is now officially named "Joey Ramone Place." He is buried in Hillside Cemetery in New Jersey, overlooking Manhattan. "he died on April 15, 2001, a month short of his 50th birthday. The corner of East Second Street in Bahri is now officially known as Joey Ramon Place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's Early Glam Phase
podcast.body: Around his 21st birthday, Joey became deeply immersed in glam culture, idolizing David Bowie and Alice Cooper. He would dress in satin jumpsuits adorned with rhinestones and wear knee-high platform boots, which exaggerated his height to six feet eight inches. "He also became a big fan of Alice Cooper. His first real band was called Sniper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's Health Issues
podcast.body: Unknown to most at the time of their retirement, Joey Ramone was suffering from lymphoma. This illness, combined with ongoing internal band tensions and his historical predisposition to colds and flu, made dealing with the rigors of performing increasingly difficult and contributed to the decision to end the band. "What we didn't know at the time was that Joy Ramon was sick. He'd been working through lymphoma and was finding it increasingly hard to deal with the rigors of performing."

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's Marfan Syndrome
podcast.body: Jeffrey Hyman (Joey Ramone) suffered from Marfan Syndrome, an inherited disorder affecting connective tissue, leading to his tall, gangly physique with long limbs and fingers. This condition can also cause serious heart problems and, if untreated, typically limits life expectancy to 32 years. "Young Jeffrey grew up with all sorts of health problems. He was tall and gauky as the result of something called Marfan Syndrome, which is an inherited disorder living on chromosome 15 that messes with connective tissue."

podcast.title: Joey Ramone's OCD
podcast.body: Diagnosed with OCD at age 18, Joey Ramone's life was plagued by the disorder. This manifested in specific rituals, such as needing to step on and off a curb a certain number of times before moving on, and elaborate routines required before leaving his apartment. "For example, he sometimes had to step on and off a curb a prescribed number of times before he could move on."

podcast.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Decades-Long Feud (Post-Linda Breakup)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone was deeply heartbroken when his girlfriend Linda left him for his bandmate Johnny Ramone, whom she later married. Joey never forgave either of them, and despite remaining in the same band until the end, Joey and Johnny reportedly never spoke to each other after Linda changed relationships, leading to a decade of silence between them during band activities. "The story is that although they were in the same band together to the end, Joey and Johnny never spoke a word to each other after Linda changed teams."

podcast.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Feud
podcast.body: A long-standing feud between Joey and Johnny Ramone was hinted at in the song "The KKK Took My Baby Away." Joey's apparent diatribe against racism may have obliquely referred to a former girlfriend, Linda, who had a dalliance with and eventually married Johnny, causing an enduring rift between the bandmates. "Joey may have been obliquely referring to a former girlfriend whom Johnny Ramone had had a dalliance with."

podcast.body: Jeffrey Hyman decided to change his stage name to Joey Ramone, believing it sounded "much cooler" than Jeff Ramon, further cementing the band's unified identity. podcast.body: An anecdote recounts Johnny Ramone attending The Beatles' concert at Shea Stadium on August 23, 1966, armed with a bag of rocks, which he then threw at the band. podcast.title: Johnny Ramone – Documented All 2,262 Ramones Gigs
podcast.body: As the Ramones' de facto leader, chief strategist, and disciplinarian, Johnny Ramone made most business decisions, dictated what everyone wore on stage, controlled practice schedules, approved every set list, and scrupulously documented every single one of the 2,262 gigs the Ramones ever played. "Johnny was the one who scrupulously documented every single one of the 2,262 gigs the Ramones ever played."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's "Straight-Edge" Lifestyle
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone ceased drug use in his early 20s, abstained from alcohol, and approached his work with the Ramones in a highly regimented, disciplined, and job-like manner. "Johnny stopped doing drugs when he was in his early 20s."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Alternative Healing Attempt
podcast.body: In an attempt to combat his cancer, Johnny Ramone underwent a few rounds of treatment with a "new age healer" from Vancouver, but these efforts proved unsuccessful. "There were also a few rounds with a new age healer from Vancouver, but that didn't work."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Cancer Progression and Pain
podcast.body: After numerous rounds of chemotherapy that caused him to go bald and feel self-conscious, scans in 2003 revealed his cancer had metastasized to his bones, lung, and bladder, leading to dangerously low blood counts and tremendous pain, which he disliked treating with painkillers. "In 2003, scans showed that the cancer had spread to his bones, his lung, and his bladder."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Catholic Upbringing Trauma
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone harbored strong negative feelings against his Catholic upbringing, claiming that he had been physically abused by nuns. "He also harbored strong feelings against his Catholic upbringing, saying that he was physically abused by nuns."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Cenotaph at Hollywood Forever Cemetery
podcast.body: Although his ashes are held by his wife Linda, a notable cenotaph dedicated to Johnny Ramone is located at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery, situated not far from D.D. Ramone's burial site. "Linda has his ashes, but there is a fantastic cenotaph at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Conservative Politics
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone was known as a hardcore Republican, one of the most conservative punk rockers. He openly admired and worshipped Ronald Reagan. This political stance often put him at odds with Joey Ramone, especially when he had to perform anti-Reagan songs written by Joey, such as "Bonzo Goes to Bitburg."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Discipline and Baseball Fandom
podcast.body: Johnny Cummings (Johnny Ramone) came from a blue-collar background and attended military schools, instilling in him a strong sense of discipline. He was a lifelong, fervent fan of the New York Yankees, with stories of him having a TV set up just off stage to watch games while performing gigs. "His parents hoped that he turned out to be a pro baseball player. And there were stories about how when there was a big game on, Johnny would have a TV set up just off stage so he could play the gig and watch the game at the same time."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Friendship with Kurt Hammett
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone was frequently visited by Kurt Hammett of Metallica, who shared a significant interest in horror movie posters with him. "He was often visited by Kurt Hammett of Metallica, who also had a major thing for horror movie posters."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Love for Baseball and Disney
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone's greatest pleasure was baseball, which explains the baseball bat prominently featured in the Ramones' logo, and he also collected cards and memorabilia related to the sport. He also enjoyed visiting Disney World and Disneyland and collected movie posters. "His greatest pleasure was baseball. And that explains the baseball bat and the Ramones logo."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Personal Collections
podcast.body: Inside his Hollywood Hills home, Johnny Ramone kept his extensive baseball collection, Disney memorabilia, movie posters, a room dedicated to Elvis, and various stuffed animals, including a two-headed calf. "Inside was his baseball collection, his Disney memorabilia, his movie posters, a room dedicated to Elvis, and a bunch of stuffed game, including a two-headed calf."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Pink Hollywood Hills Ranch House
podcast.body: At the time of his illness, Johnny Ramone resided in a pink-painted, gated ranch house in the Hollywood Hills, partially financed by the sale of some of his renowned guitars, one of which fetched $937,000. "By this time, he was living in a gated ranch house up on the Hollywood hills that was painted pink, something that was partly financed by selling some of his famous guitars."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Political Views
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone was a staunch political conservative, an unusual stance for a punk musician, openly supporting Ronald Reagan, both Bushes, and identifying as a major Republican. "Johnny was a hardcore political conservative. He loved Ronald Reagan and both Bushes and was a major Republican supporter."

podcast.title: Johnny Ramone's Post-Mortem Sentiments
podcast.body: Johnny Ramone expressed his lack of desire to interact with Joey Ramone even in death, stating he wouldn't want Joey at his funeral and wouldn't want to hear from him if he were dying, preferring to be left alone by friends. podcast.title: Love Triangle and Intra-Band Feud
podcast.body: In 1976, Joey Ramone met 16-year-old fan Linda Danielle from Queens at CBGB. They reconnected in Los Angeles a couple of years later and became a couple, with Linda joining The Ramones on tour. Johnny Ramone, who initially made Linda sit in the back of the van, eventually discovered common ground with her (neither drank or did drugs, she liked to cook, he liked home-cooked meals) and they became best friends. Joey and Linda became engaged, but after a dispute over a ring price, Johnny realized he was in love with Linda. Johnny intimidated Joey, who hated conflict, leading Linda to move towards Johnny over the next 18 months. They broke up, and Johnny and Linda became a couple in the early 1980s, marrying in 1984. "In 1976, just as the Ramones were starting to become known, Joey met a young 16-year-old fan named Linda Danielle."

podcast.title: Mainstream Perception vs. Importance
podcast.body: Although the mainstream treated The Ramones as a joke for decades, they were, in fact, one of the most important bands rock and roll had ever seen. Their foundational influence is noted as essential for bands like Green Day, Nirvana, The Offspring, and Pearl Jam.

podcast.title: Mainstream Radio Blackout
podcast.body: In 1978, mainstream radio stations in America refused to play Ramones records, deeming punk rock "too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, too political." The American music industry largely considered punk a fad to be ignored until it disappeared. "Mainstream radio stations wouldn't touch punk rock. podcast.title: Major Label Punk

"And weren't the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and the Clash all in major labels?"

podcast.body: The Ramones' musical template was characterized by loud, fast, and fuzzy sounds, essentially "amped up 60 style pop songs." Their style featured simple, sing-along melodies, no overt political messages, no guitar solos, and strict adherence to songs under three minutes in length. "But if you really pay attention, there's nothing more than really amped up 60 style pop songs."

podcast.title: Name Origin (Paul McCartney Connection)
podcast.body: The band's chosen surname, "Ramone," was inspired by Dee Dee Ramone's admiration for Paul McCartney. During his time with The Silver Beatles, McCartney would use the alias "Paul Ramone" to check into hotel rooms. Dee Dee, already calling himself Dee Dee Ramone, suggested "The Ramones" for the band to signify unity and family. "DD was a big fan of Paul McCartney and the Beatles, and the days of the Silver Beatles, Paul McCartney used to check on two hotel rooms using the alias Paul Ramone."

podcast.title: Nancy Spungen as Groupie – Followed the Band
podcast.body: Nancy Spungen was a hardcore groupie who followed the Ramones during her time in New York before moving to England. "She became a hardcore groupie following the remones."

podcast.title: New Wave Marketing Strategy
podcast.body: At a Sire Records marketing meeting, it was suggested to use the term "new wave" in place of "punk" to describe their new signings, including The Ramones. This strategic rebranding effectively removed the stigmas associated with punk, allowing their music to gain acceptance. "And so it came to pass that at a marketing meeting at Sire Records, someone suggested that they use the term new wave in place of punk to describe their new signings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Punk and Apolitical Stance
podcast.body: Originating in New York, the Ramones were part of the early punk scene, which catered to artsy outsiders. While there was some general rebellion, the Ramones, alongside other major players like Blondie and the Talking Heads, were not notably political in their musical output. "if you look at the major players, like the Ramones and Blondie and the Talking Heds, none of them were very political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Openness to Pop Influences
podcast.body: Unlike some early punk bands that professed disdain for previous generations, The Ramones were open about their pop sensibilities and expressed no issues with iconic popular acts like The Beatles, The Beach Boys, Motown, or 60s girl groups. They frequently covered 60s pop songs, overtly demonstrating their appreciation for the genre. "The Ramones definitely a punk band, but under the surface, they were also very much a pop band."

podcast.title: Origin of Sound
podcast.body: Tommy Ramone stated that the band's distinctive sound arose from a desire to play music that wasn't heard on the radio, leading them to create it themselves. "We used to sit around and listen to the radio and not hear anything like the stuff we like So we decided to play it ourselves."

podcast.title: Origin of the Band Name
podcast.body: Douglas Colvin, a huge Paul McCartney fan, knew McCartney sometimes used the alias "Paul Ramon" (after producer Phil Ramon) on hotel registers. Douglas adopted "D.D. Ramon." The plural, "Ramones," sounded like a gang, and as no other names clicked, it stuck. To reinforce a "gang mentality," all members adopted "Ramone" as their surname, deciding to appear as brothers, and wore leather jackets, jeans, and t-shirts. "Douglas liked the sound of that, so he started calling himself D.D. Ramon... The plural of Ramon, Ramon's, sounded like it could be the name of a gang."

podcast.title: Original Lineup and Roles
podcast.body: The initial lineup included Jeff Hyman (Joey Ramone) on drums, a "6'6-inch skinny guy" and "OCD-suffering refugee from a failed band called Sniper." Their first gig was in March. By July, Jeff Hyman moved to lead vocals because he was a better singer than drummer, and their manager, Tommy (Tommy Ramone), a recording engineer who had worked with Jimi Hendrix, took over on drums. "Their drummer was a 6'6-inch skinny guy named Jeff Heimann, an OCD-suffering refugee from a failed band called Sniper."

podcast.body: In their early days, The Ramones faced arguments backstage because audience members would complain they didn't play long enough, often only 45 minutes instead of the contracted hour. xref.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
xref.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. xref.title: First Show October 17, 1975 – Pre-dates Sex Pistols and The Clash; 1980 Ontario Place Riot
xref.body: Teenage Head formed in Hamilton, Ontario, and played their first show on October 17, 1975 at Westdale High School — three weeks before the Sex Pistols played their first gig, and nine months before The Clash formed. They were a major force in Canadian punk, combining elements of the Ramones, New York Dolls, and 1950s rock and roll. Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

xref.title: Murder at Chelsea Hotel (October 12, 1978)
xref.body: Nancy Spungen, girlfriend of Sid Vicious, was found dead from a single stab wound to her stomach in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Nancy had a troubled life, diagnosed with schizophrenia at 15 and supporting herself through prostitution from age 17 before becoming a groupie to bands like The Ramones, New York Dolls, and Aerosmith. She became inseparable from Sid Vicious for 19 months, and they both were heroin and Tuinal addicts. On the night of October 11, 1978, several people visited their room, and Sid allegedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, completely incapacitating him. At around 2:30 am on October 12th, Nancy asked Rockets Redglare, their drug connection and Sid's bodyguard, for Dilaudid. Later, around 7:30 am, female moans were heard, and at 10 am, Sid called the front desk. Nancy was found stabbed and bleeding to death, in a weird angle under the bathroom sink. Sid initially confessed but was likely too incapacitated. The theory later emerged that Rockets Redglare, who died in 2007, was the murderer, allegedly stabbing Nancy with Sid's Bowie knife during an argument over stolen cash, a confession he reportedly made while drinking at CBGB. "Nancy Spungin, girlfriend of ex-sex Bristol Sidvicious, at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978."

xref.title: Joey Ramone's OCD – Lifelong Battle Barely Acknowledged, Finally Confirmed on 2002 Solo Album
xref.body: Joey Ramone suffered from obsessive-compulsive disorder that preceded the formation of the Ramones and is cited by those close to him as a major reason he was so shy, awkward, and withdrawn in private. His OCD manifested in compulsive repetitive behaviors — stepping off and on a curb dozens of times, repeating words over and over driven by voices in his head — and he was hospitalized at least once when it became unmanageable. Despite this, Joey vehemently denied having OCD whenever it was raised publicly, and the subject was almost never discussed. As he came to terms with his cancer and mortality, he relented slightly, and in the song "Like a Drug I Never Did Before" on his 2002 posthumous solo album *Don't Worry About Me*, he addressed his lifelong battle with OCD — the only time he ever mentioned it in his music. xref.title: Camden Rehearsal Space
xref.body: The band rehearsed in a building in Camden, which notably featured a jukebox. The Clash particularly favored Dub music, identifying it as the music of the immigrant communities with whom they shared their neighborhood. xref.title: Catalyst for British Punk Explosion
xref.body: The Ramones' two London gigs in July 1976 are considered foundational for the British punk rock explosion. Major figures like Johnny Rotten, Sid Vicious, Joe Strummer, Chrissy Hynde, The Damned, and Billy Idol were in attendance and were profoundly "transformed by what they saw and heard," inspiring them to form their own bands. "Over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

xref.title: Early Rehearsals and Lineup Changes
xref.body: The Ramones' first rehearsal took place at Johnny's apartment with bassist Richie Stern, who quickly quit. A more formal rehearsal followed on January 24th, 1974, at the Performance Studio, with Jeffrey on drums, Johnny on guitar, and Douglas on lead vocals and bass. They were initially "terrible," unable to play their instruments well or covers, only knowing their own simple songs. Douglas quickly lost his voice, and Jeffrey, a loud but slow drummer, moved to vocals, leading to Tommy eventually taking over drums in July 1974. "They were not ready, not even close. They had next to no idea how to play their instruments."

xref.title: Early Rehearsals and Ramones Covers
xref.body: In their initial stages, Husker Dü honed their craft by playing covers of Ramones songs during rehearsals, often taking place in bassist Greg Norton's basement. This grounding in punk rock was combined with their later pop sensibilities. "And while the same time Husker Do was stumbling through remones covers during their first rehearsals and bassist Greg Norton's basement, another important Minneapolis band was coming together in a basement on Bryant Street South."

xref.title: Early Residency at CBGB
xref.body: Television began playing a regular Sunday Night Residency at Hilly Crystal's bar, which would soon become widely known as CBGB. Their performances, starting around the same time that displaced artists from the Mercer Art Center began migrating to CBGB, helped establish the club as a hub for new music in New York City. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

xref.title: Early Sire Records Signing
xref.body: The Ramones were among the new bands signed by Seymour Stein, head of Sire Records, who was a fan of the emerging scene at CBGB in New York. "The head of the company, a guy named Seymour Stein, was a fan of what was happening at CBGB and had signed a bunch of these new bands, including the Ramones."

xref.title: Early Songwriting Themes
xref.body: The Ramones began writing songs about what they knew, which largely involved being "near-to-wells" and "hoodlums" who were better at "hanging out, drinking, getting in fist fights, and doing drugs" than actual crime. Their early songs often began with the phrase "I don't want to," such as "I Don't Want To Get Involved With You," "I Don't Want To Walk Around With You," "I Don't Want To Be Learned, I Don't Want To Be Tamed," and "I Don't Want To Go Down To The Basement." "They started to write about what they knew, which was, well what exactly? Well, they were all a bunch of near-to-wells, a bunch of hoodlums."

xref.title: Early UK Punk Performance
xref.body: Patty Smith, referred to as a "punk priestess," played a show in England a couple of months before The Ramones' July 1976 appearances. Her performance was one of the few instances of US-style punk rock exposure in the UK before the Ramones' more significant impact. "Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."

xref.title: Enduring Animosity
xref.body: Despite Johnny Ramone and Linda Danielle marrying in 1984, The Ramones remained together and continued touring until 1996. Joey Ramone did not speak to Linda again until 1993, and he and Johnny almost never spoke again until the band's breakup. The feud was intense and quiet, prioritizing the band's business over personal issues. Johnny did not contact Joey when he was dying in early 2000 nor attend his funeral. "Joey didn't speak to Linda again until 1993. And Joey and Johnny almost never spoke again."

xref.body: Even though the Ramones never sold many records, they are now regarded as one of the most important rock bands ever. Their signing to Sire Records was a pivotal moment for indie music. xref.title: Evolution from Hardcore to Power Pop
xref.body: The Replacements initially started as a hardcore act, heavily influenced by punk bands like the Ramones, Sex Pistols, and New York Dolls. Over time, they became more melodic and adopted more conventional song structures, influenced by The Rolling Stones, The Beatles, and CCR, eventually evolving into a power pop band. "They recorded for a label called Twin Tone and were very much a hardcore-acted first. Their heroes were the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and the New York Dolls. But as things went on, they became more melodic and their songs had more conventional structures thanks to their love for the Rolling Stones and the Beatles and CCR. Leader Paul Westorberg grew into a very accomplished songwriter and the longer the bands stayed together, the more they became a power pop band."

xref.title: Extensive Influences
xref.body: Weezer's influences are broad and deep within the Powerpop lineage, including foundational bands like The Beatles, The Ramones, Cheap Trick, The Knack, and The Cars, as well as The Pixies. This wide array of influences supports the argument that they are currently the leading Powerpop band in the world. "Their influences include the Beatles, the Ramones, Cheap Trick, the Nack, the Cars, the Pixies, ensure just about every single band that we've mentioned so far."

xref.title: Extensive Touring and Performances
xref.body: The band has a reputation for playing a vast number of shows, appearing "anywhere and everywhere" asked by their label or radio stations, including pop-up gigs and spontaneous busking. They estimate they've played hundreds of shows per year for over a decade, working between 175 and 200 days annually on musically directed activities. This volume of performance is suggested to have potentially surpassed the Ramones' lifetime total of 2250 shows. "We do say we do like a hundred a year for, we've been doing this for 12 years. 1200 shows."

xref.title: Final Gig and Legacy
xref.body: The Ramones' official end came on August 6, 1996, after a gig at The Palace in Hollywood. Over their 22-year career, they played 2,236 gigs since their first performance as a trio in March 1974. They are often called the "Johnny Apple Seeds of Rock" for inspiring thousands of new bands wherever they played. "until the official end of the band on August 6, 1996 after a gig at the palace in Hollywood. 22 years and 2,236 gigs since that first performance as a trio in March of 1974."

xref.title: First to Crossover to Mainstream
xref.body: R.E.M. is recognized as one of the first and largest bands from the college/alternative rock scene to successfully cross over into mainstream consciousness. Their success helped popularize "alternative" as an umbrella term for distinct rock music. "I guess REM was the first and the biggest, the word alternative became more widely used as this umbrella term for rock music that was different that did not descend from the Beatles and the Stones and Led Zeppelin, but from Bowie and Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground and the Ramones."

xref.title: Florence Welch's Artistic and Academic Family Background
xref.body: Florence Leontine Mary Welch comes from a highly artistic, literary, and academic family. Her father is an advertising executive who encouraged her to explore diverse music, moving beyond Ramones records. Her mother is a highly educated academic, holding positions at institutions like Harvard, Warburg, University of London, and King's College London, and is a professor of Renaissance studies, which informed Florence's artistic aesthetic. Her uncle is a renowned satirist, freelance journalist for British newspapers, broadcaster, and TV writer, while an aunt served as an editor of The Daily Telegraph. "Florence, Leontine, Mary Welch. Dad is an advertising executive who insisted that Florence put away the Ramones records and tried different music. Mom is an academic, Harvard, Warburg, University of London, King's College London. And she's a professor of Renaissance studies."

xref.title: Formation and Lineup Change – Drummer to Frontman
xref.body: The Ramones were formed in early 1974, with Jeff Hyman (later Joey Ramone) on drums, John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) on guitar, and Douglas Colvin (later D.D. Ramone) on bass. Their first gig was on March 30, 1974. Due to Jeff's powerful, fast drumming style and his superior singing ability, he transitioned to lead vocalist, with a friend named Tommy taking over on drums using a basic $100 kit. "This arrangements worked out pretty good Especially after John became Johnny and Douglas became D.D. and Jeff adopted the name Joey and they all adopted the same last name Ramon."

xref.title: Founding Partners and Previous Bands
xref.body: Shane MacGowan and Spider Stacy met in the toilets at a Ramones show at the Roundhouse in London in 1977. Both had previously been members of several other bands, including The Nippley Rectors (later shortened to The Nipps), the Millwall Chain Saws, and the New Republicans, before forming The Pogues in 1982. "Shane's co-founding partner was Spider Stacy, a guy he met in the toilets at a Ramone show at the Roundhouse in London in 1977. Both had been in several bands with names like The Nippley Rectors, later shortened to just The Nipps, plus they were in the Millwall Chain Saws and the new Republicans."

xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

xref.title: Godfather of Grunge
xref.body: Neil Young is recognized as the "godfather of Grunge," particularly in Seattle where he was a big favorite. His career phase in the 1970s, characterized by "obnoxiously overdriven guitar grinding under a simple melody" and a "calculated sloppiness," held a specific appeal that deeply resonated with and influenced the burgeoning Seattle music scene. "If Iggy Pop was the godfather of punk, the Ramones, with the Johnny Apples seeds of alt rock, well then Neil Young, a big favorite in Seattle, is the godfather of Grunge."

xref.title: Godfathers of the Sound
xref.body: The Ramones are referred to as "one of the British Godfathers of this sound," specifically in the context of Powerpop and its integration with punk and new wave, indicating their foundational role despite being an American band often associated with punk. "Of course, we can't forget the Ramones in all this. One of the British Godfathers of this sound was Nick Lowe..." (Clarification: The text says "One of the British Godfathers of this sound was Nick Lowe," directly after mentioning The Ramones. It's likely intended to mean The Ramones as a godfather of *a* sound, and then pivoting to Nick Lowe as *a* British godfather, not that The Ramones were British godfathers). The Ramones are better categorized as a key influence *on* the sound without the "British" qualifier here. "Of course, we can't forget the Ramones in all this."

xref.title: Image and Sound
xref.body: The Ramones were known for their quintessential punk image, characterized by leather jackets and torn jeans, and for playing music that was really fast and really loud. However, beneath this surface, their musical core was deeply influenced by the pop radio of the 1960s, essentially playing their unique version of pop songs. "The pop radio of the 1960s was a huge influence of the Ramones."
